name: Dutch Defense
summary: The Dutch Defense (1.d4 f5) grabs kingside space and fights for e4 via the Classical, Stonewall, and Leningrad setups.
intro: The Dutch Defense answers 1.d4 with the combative 1...f5, immediately staking a claim on the kingside and fighting for control of e4. After a typical 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 e6 4.Nf3 Be7, Black chooses among three time-honoured setups — the Classical, the Stonewall, and the Leningrad — each giving the opening its own character while accepting a slight loosening of the king's position.
line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 e6 Nf3 Be7

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: With 1...f5 Black fights for the e4-square and gains kingside space, typically aiming for a later ...e5 break or a direct attack against the enemy king. The cost is a slight loosening of the position: the move weakens e6 and the a2-g8 and h5-e8 diagonals, so White most often fianchettoes with g3 and Bg2 to press along the long light diagonal and probe the resulting soft squares.

The choice of setup defines the middlegame structure. The Classical (...e6, ...d6, ...Be7) keeps things flexible and prepares ...e5; the Stonewall (...d5, ...e6, ...c6 alongside the f5-pawn) clamps down on e4 and the dark squares but leaves the c8-bishop passive and concedes the e5-outpost; the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6) fianchettoes on the kingside and strikes with ...e5, resembling a King's Indian with reversed emphasis.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: Against White's main try, the fianchetto with 2.g3, Black selects one of the three principal systems. In the Stonewall, Black builds the d5-e6-f5 pawn wall and often reroutes the light-squared bishop via ...Bd7-e8-h5; in the Leningrad, ...g6 and ...Bg7 support the thematic ...e5; in the Classical, flexible development keeps both the ...e5 break and a kingside attack in reserve.

White also has sharp anti-Dutch tries that avoid the fianchetto. The Staunton Gambit, 2.e4, offers a pawn for rapid development and open lines, while 2.Bg5 and 2.Nc3 aim to enforce e4, and early moves like 2.h3 with g4 challenge the f5-pawn directly. Each of these attempts to exploit the slight weaknesses created by ...f5 before Black completes his setup.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The opening owes its name to Elias Stein, an author based in the Netherlands who recommended 1...f5 in a treatise published in the late eighteenth century. Long regarded as a fighting, double-edged reply to 1.d4, the Dutch has been employed at the highest level — Mikhail Botvinnik was a notable champion of both its Stonewall and Classical forms — and it remains a favourite of players seeking an unbalanced struggle with the black pieces.

white: Fianchetto with g3 and Bg2 to control the long light diagonal.
Target the weakened e6-square and the light squares near Black's king.
Consider the Staunton Gambit 2.e4 or 2.Bg5 to exploit ...f5 early.
Challenge Black's grip on e4 and pry open lines toward the king.
Exchange Black's good bishop to leave the weakened squares exposed.
black: Choose a setup — Classical, Stonewall, or Leningrad — to taste.
Fight for the e4-square and prepare the freeing ...e5 advance.
In the Leningrad, fianchetto ...g6 and ...Bg7 and expand on the kingside.
In the Stonewall, clamp e4 and reroute the c8-bishop via ...Be8-h5.
Launch a kingside attack once White has castled short.
